`, which wins because it has more words than 0. Longer cards (wrapper over 200 words) extract fine. A possible direction: let a block that holds the page's `

` / main paragraphs escape the navigation-heading exit, or reject a hidden-selector retry whose result is almost entirely link text.
title: Short page body removed when its wrapper has a "Comments" heading; hidden-content retry then returns a hidden link list

Parsing a GitHub gist page with a long file takes minutes, and a big enough one never finishes. I hit this in a server that runs Defuddle on fetched pages. A 10 MB gist kept the process at 100% CPU until I attached a debugger to find out why. ## Real World Case It's happened with smaller gists, but just as an example the [20K English Words](https://gist.github.com/eyturner/3d56f6a194f411af9f29df4c9d4a4e6e) gist (4.9 MB of HTML, 19,999 lines) takes 309 s with the CLI: ``` curl -s -A "Mozilla/5.0" -o gist.html https://gist.github.com/eyturner/3d56f6a194f411af9f29df4c9d4a4e6e npx defuddle@0.19.5 parse gist.html ``` ## Reproduction Case A table shaped like a gist's code view reproduces it: ```js import { parseHTML } from 'linkedom'; import { Defuddle } from 'defuddle/node'; const rows = Array.from({ length: 8000 }, (_, i) => `${i + 1}const value${i} = ${i};`).join('\n'); const html = `
\n${rows}\n
`; const t = performance.now(); await Defuddle(parseHTML(html).document, 'https://example.com/'); console.log(Math.round(performance.now() - t), 'ms'); ``` The time roughly quadruples each time the row count doubles, with both linkedom and jsdom: | Rows | linkedom | jsdom | |---|---|---| | 1,000 | 0.3 s | 3.7 s | | 2,000 | 0.9 s | 13.1 s | | 4,000 | 3.4 s | 49.8 s | | 8,000 | 12.5 s | over 120 s | Each figure is a single run, on Windows 11 with Node 24.12, defuddle 0.19.5, linkedom 0.18.13 and jsdom 29.1.1. 0.19.4 behaves the same. In the stack samples from the stuck process, every sample was in `extractStructuredText` in `elements/code.js`, inside the `parentElement?.querySelector('[data-line], .line')` call on text nodes.

Some blog themes put a `data-date` attribute on the element that wraps the entire post body. For example, a Ghost site with a custom theme does this (the live page below): ```html

Post title

8 April 2025

First paragraph…

Second paragraph…

``` `[data-date]` in `EXACT_SELECTORS` matches the wrapper, so `removeBySelector` deletes the whole body and the result is an empty `
` (wordCount 0). None of the retries in `_parseWithRetries` turn exact selectors off, so the content is never recovered. The selected main content is protected only against removing itself or an ancestor, and here the wrapper is a descendant. **Reproduce** - `curl https://defuddle.md/https://felixrieseberg.com/how-to-be-more-ambitious-a-tutorial-for-humans-with-models/` returns frontmatter and no body. - `npx defuddle@0.19.5 parse https://felixrieseberg.com/how-to-be-more-ambitious-a-tutorial-for-humans-with-models/ --md` prints `Error: No content could be extracted`. - Removing only the `data-date` attribute from the wrapper returns the full post (about 2,200 words). Reproduced on 0.19.5 and on main (556d74e). **Proposed fix** The selector is meant for date badges, which never contain paragraphs. The header rule already handles the same problem with `header:not(:has(p + p))`. I'll open a PR that changes the rule to `[data-date]:not(:has(p ~ p))` (`~` rather than `+`, so paragraphs separated by headings still count), with a fixture. **Question: the other metadata selectors** `.date`, `#date`, `.author`, `.Author`, `.contributor`, `.entry-meta`, `.meta`, `.tags`, `#tags`, `.headline` and `#headline` assume the same thing: the matched element is small. A content wrapper that happens to carry one of these class names would lose its body the same way. I haven't seen a real page that does this, so the PR only changes `[data-date]`. Adding the same `:not(:has(p ~ p))` guard to all eleven leaves every existing fixture unchanged (linkedom and jsdom). Would you like that in the same PR, or a separate one?
title: [data-date] removes the whole post body when the content wrapper carries data-date

## Empty-element cleanup removes structural MathML nodes

Defuddle 0.19.5 / upstream `556d74e8`, Node API with LinkeDOM 0.18.12 (also observed in the LinkeDOM-based Worker).

`removeEmptyElements()` applies HTML emptiness rules inside `<math>`. For example, in an article paragraph:

```html
<!-- before -->
<math><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>k</mi></msub></math>
<!-- extracted subtree -->
<math><msub><mi>k</mi></msub></math>
```

The empty `<mrow>` is the base argument, not disposable whitespace. Removing it leaves `msub` with one child instead of its required base/subscript pair. Empty `none`, `mprescripts`, `mspace`, and `mtd` nodes are likewise meaningful placeholders, prescript boundaries, spacing, or matrix cells.

Real example: https://arxiv.org/html/2609.38986v1, equation `S2.E5.m1`, contains `<msub><mrow></mrow><mi>k</mi></msub>`; its empty base is lost in extracted HTML and Worker MathML output. A separate LaTeX source can conceal this loss in Markdown, so checking HTML structure matters.

Expected: do not remove MathML descendants solely because they contain no text. Ordinary empty HTML and a completely empty `<math>` with no descendants or source should still be removable. This report is limited to empty-element cleanup, not general MathML preservation or wrapper/table normalization (e.g. #377, #141).
title: Empty-element cleanup removes structural MathML descendants

body:
### Summary

`BilibiliExtractor` never produces a transcript when Defuddle runs inside a **Firefox** browser extension content script (e.g. Obsidian Web Clipper). The same code works on Chrome.

Root cause: the extractor sets the **forbidden request-header** `User-Agent` on its `fetch()` calls. Chrome silently strips it (per the Fetch spec), so the request stays a *simple* request. Firefox actually sends it, which makes the request *non-simple*, so the browser issues a **CORS preflight** — and Bilibili's subtitle CDN answers `OPTIONS` with **405** and no CORS headers. The subtitle JSON is therefore never retrieved, and the extractor returns `undefined` silently.

**Impact:** every Obsidian Web Clipper user on Firefox/Zen who clips a Bilibili video gets an empty transcript (Chrome users are unaffected). The same `User-Agent` header is set by other extractors in the shipped bundle as well (for example the Reddit one, when fetching `old.reddit.com`), so they are exposed to the same class of failure.

### Where

`src/extractors/bilibili.ts`

Three call sites set the header. Only the third one is fatal, because it targets a host that does not implement CORS preflight:

```ts
// fetchViewData()  - ok in practice, api.bilibili.com answers preflight correctly
const response = await this.fetch(url, {
    headers: {
        'Accept': 'application/json',
        'User-Agent': 'Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; Defuddle/1.0)',
    },
    credentials: 'include' as RequestCredentials,
    signal: AbortSignal.timeout(FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS),
});

// fetchPlayerV2()  - same pattern
const response = await this.fetch(url, {
    headers: {
        'Accept': 'application/json',
        'User-Agent': 'Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; Defuddle/1.0)',
    },
    credentials: 'include' as RequestCredentials,
    signal: AbortSignal.timeout(FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS),
});

// fetchTranscript() - the one that fails: subtitle file on aisubtitle.hdslb.com
const subtitleResponse = await this.fetch(subtitleUrl.toString(), {
    headers: {
        'Accept': 'application/json',
        'User-Agent': 'Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; Defuddle/1.0)',
    },
    signal: AbortSignal.timeout(FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS),
});
if (!subtitleResponse.ok) {
    return undefined;   // <- the 405 lands here and is swallowed
}
```

`Accept` is CORS-safelisted, so **removing just the `User-Agent` header is enough** to make the request simple again and fix it.

### Why this is browser-specific

| | Chrome | Firefox |
|---|---|---|
| `User-Agent` is a forbidden header name (Fetch spec) | silently dropped | **actually sent** by extension content scripts |
| Resulting request | simple request | **non-simple -> needs preflight** |
| Does the browser send `OPTIONS`? | no | **yes** |
| Subtitle CDN response | `200` + `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` | **`405`** with **no** CORS headers |
| Transcript | works | **silently empty** |

### Reproduction

1. Obsidian Web Clipper 1.7.1 on Firefox (157.0) / Zen (1.23b, same Gecko), logged in to bilibili.com.
2. Clip any Bilibili video that has an AI subtitle track (`api.bilibili.com/x/player/v2` -> `data.subtitle.subtitles` is non-empty).
3. The transcript is empty. Repeating with a page reload gives **0/5**.
4. The identical extension build in Chrome gives **5/5**.

Observed on the wire (via `webRequest` on a real profile; Defuddle's own requests are recognisable by the custom User-Agent):

```
SEND https://api.bilibili.com/x/web-interface/view?bvid=BV...                -> 200
SEND https://api.bilibili.com/x/player/wbi/v2?bvid=...&aid=...&cid=...      -> 200
SEND https://api.bilibili.com/x/player/v2?bvid=...&cid=...                  -> 200
SEND https://aisubtitle.hdslb.com/bfs/ai_subtitle/prod/11337264110548526470449592b2...
RECV status=405   (no Access-Control-Allow-* headers)
     error NS_ERROR_DOM_BAD_URI
```

The three API calls succeed (that host implements CORS properly) and the subtitle track **is** returned — only the final subtitle download fails.

### Verification against the CDN

```bash
# simple GET -> works
curl -i 'https://aisubtitle.hdslb.com/bfs/ai_subtitle/prod/<id>' \
     -H 'Origin: https://www.bilibili.com'
# => HTTP 200, Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *

# preflight -> always fails, for any Access-Control-Request-Headers value
curl -i -X OPTIONS 'https://aisubtitle.hdslb.com/bfs/ai_subtitle/prod/<id>' \
     -H 'Origin: https://www.bilibili.com' \
     -H 'Access-Control-Request-Method: GET' \
     -H 'Access-Control-Request-Headers: user-agent'
# => HTTP 405, and ACAO / ACAH / ACAM are all absent
```

(`<id>` comes from `subtitle_url` returned by `x/player/v2`.)

### Suggested fix

Drop the `User-Agent` header from these `fetch()` calls (or set it only when running outside a browser, since Defuddle also runs under Node where it is meaningful). There are 8 occurrences of this header in the shipped Web Clipper `content.js`; 3 of them are in this extractor. The same pattern also appears in other extractors (for example the Reddit one fetches `old.reddit.com` with the same header), so those are likely to hit the same class of problem in Firefox.

### Related issue in the same file

`BilibiliExtractor.transcriptCache` **caches failures**, which turns a transient failure into a sticky one:

```ts
transcript = await this.fetchTranscript(aid, cid, bvid);
if (cacheKey) {
    BilibiliExtractor.transcriptCache.set(cacheKey, transcript ?? null);
```

The cache key is `bvid:cid:language` and the map lives for the lifetime of the module, so after one failure **every subsequent extraction in that page returns no transcript until the page is reloaded**. Since `x/player/v2` sometimes legitimately returns an empty `subtitles` array (I measured roughly 50% on repeated requests for the same video with a valid login), this makes the feature look permanently broken. Only successful results should be cached.

### Environment

- Firefox 157.0 and Zen 1.23b (Windows 11); Chrome 154 for comparison
- Defuddle as bundled in Obsidian Web Clipper 1.7.1 (the `src/extractors/bilibili.ts` code on `main` matches the shipped bundle)
- Reported from the Web Clipper side; its issue form redirects missing-content issues here.
title: BilibiliExtractor sets the forbidden User-Agent header on its fetches, which makes the transcript download fail in Firefox (CORS preflight -> 405 from the subtitle CDN)

When an `` sits inside a ``, the picture rule in `src/elements/images.ts` overwrites the image's `src` with `extractFirstUrlFromSrcset()` of the best ``. Since srcsets are usually listed smallest-first, `parse().content` ends up pointing at the thumbnail. This happens even when the original `` was already the full-size image, and even though the rule's comment says it is meant to get the highest resolution. c5adda3 (from #177) made the Markdown conversion prefer the widest srcset candidate. The HTML output still has this problem, so anyone who consumes `content` as HTML gets the smallest rendition. **Repro (defuddle 0.19.4, linkedom):** ```js const u = (w) => `https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!abc!,w_${w},c_limit,f_webp,q_auto:good/https%3A%2F%2Fexample.com%2Fimage.png`; const html = `

Post

${'Text. '.repeat(100)}

${'Text. '.repeat(100)}

`; const doc = new DOMParser().parseFromString(html, 'text/html'); new Defuddle(doc, { url: 'https://example.substack.com/p/post' }).parse().content; // — the original src was w_1456 ``` This affects every Substack post, and any site that serves `` with ascending `srcset`. **Expected:** the picture rule picks the widest candidate (the same selection the Markdown path now uses), or keeps the ``'s own `src` when it's valid. Related: #315 deals with the same rule, where it overwrites a valid `src` when the `` srcset has no descriptors.
title: `<picture>` handling sets `img src` to the smallest srcset candidate in HTML output

body: When using the Obsidian Web Clipper on blogs and websites generated with [Quarto](https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli), defuddle fails to capture and parse specific content elements correctly. First: Table headings are **always** lost: The elements (or table headers) are stripped out during the clipping process, resulting in incomplete markdown tables. Second: Multiple images are **always** truncated: If a page contains multiple images positioned next to each other (e.g., side-by-side figure grids), the clipper only successfully extracts and imports the first image in the sequence, dropping the subsequent adjacent images. **URLs where the bug occurs** https://learningstatisticswithr.com/05-descriptives.html (and generally other sites built with the Quarto publishing system) **To reproduce** - Go to https://learningstatisticswithr.com/05-descriptives.html - Use Obsidian Web Clipper & open the saved Obsidian note - Scroll to the section "5.1.1 The Mean": Notice that the table headings are missing. - Scroll to the section "5.3 Skew and Kurtosis" where three side-by-side images were present on the original webpage and notice the missing two images.
title: Defuddle loses table headings and adjacent images on Quarto-generated pages

## Request

Please support already-rendered YouTube comments and expanded replies when `includeReplies: true` is enabled. This would make YouTube page extraction useful for analyzing viewer feedback, in addition to the video description and transcript.

This request is limited to comments already present in the loaded document. It does not require automatically scrolling, expanding replies, or fetching all comments.

## Observed behavior

Tested with unpatched **Defuddle 0.19.3** in a Chrome extension, using synchronous extraction of a copy of the loaded page document.

Example: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jNQXAC9IVRw

1. Open the video and scroll to the comments section.
2. Wait for comments to render. In our repeated check, 16 non-empty visible `ytd-comment-thread-renderer #content-text` elements were present.
3. Extract the page with `includeReplies: true`.
4. Compare each loaded comment's text with the resulting Markdown.

**Actual:** 0 of the 16 loaded comments appeared in the output. The extension's output was 451 characters including its own title/source metadata, and contained video metadata/description but no comments. The result was not truncated. An earlier run with 2 loaded comments also retained neither comment.

**Expected:** include the loaded comment bodies, with author names and reply nesting where available. `includeReplies: false` should continue to exclude them.

The exact comment count and video description may change over time; the important distinction is that comments were already rendered before extraction, rather than missing because they had not loaded yet.

## Configuration

```ts
import Defuddle from 'defuddle/full';

const result = new Defuddle(pageDocumentCopy, {
  url: pageUrl,
  markdown: true,
  useAsync: false,
  includeReplies: true,
  removeLowScoring: false,
  removePartialSelectors: false,
  removeContentPatterns: false,
  standardize: false,
  removeExactSelectors: true,
  removeHiddenElements: true,
}).parse();
```

Here `pageDocumentCopy` is an inert copy of the already-loaded browser document, not HTML obtained through a separate HTTP request.

## Implementation observation

In the installed 0.19.3 YouTube extractor, `buildResult()` builds the video embed and description, then appends the transcript when available. It does not collect comment elements or consult `includeReplies`. This appears to be missing functionality rather than a lazy-loading or output-size issue.

It would be useful to reuse the shared comment formatting used by other extractors, preserving author, body, and parent/reply relationships. Suggested regression cases: loaded top-level comments, expanded replies, `includeReplies: false`, and a page without loaded comments. Existing video description/transcript extraction should remain intact.

## Summary Same-site links can be incorrectly deleted from extracted content when their target path partially matches the page's path. The check also ignores the host, so a link to a different site can be deleted whenever its target path prefixes the page's path. The link text goes with it, leaving a gap mid-sentence and no indication that anything was removed. ## Context Originally seen using: - Obsidian Web Clipper: 1.7.1 - Firefox: 156.0a1 (2026-08-25) - macOS: 26.6.2 (25G83) Reproduced using: - `defuddle` 0.19.3 - `linkedom` as the DOM backend ## Background The Obsidian Web Clipper was used to save a page who's URL looked like: ``` https://pages.example.com/acmelabs/posts/12345 ``` a link within the document, in this case referencing a different host, was incorrectly removed: ``` https://social.example.net/acme ``` ## Expected Behaviour Links within prose should be preserved unless they are section breadcrumbs or back-navigation links; the link above is neither. The docblock for the "section breadcrumb" rule in `removeByContentPattern` (`src/removals/content-patterns.ts`) states: ``` // Remove section breadcrumbs and back-navigation links. // Matches short elements (div, span, p) containing a link to a parent path, // and bare elements used as standalone back links (e.g. "← back", "↑ index"). // Two parent-link patterns are recognized: // 1. Direct prefix: linkPath is a path prefix of the current URL // e.g. current=/blog/2024/post, link=/blog/ or /blog // ... ``` So a link should only be removed when its target path is made up of _complete segments_ of the page's path: `/blog` and `/blog/2024` are parents of `/blog/2024/post`, `/blog/20` is not. It should also be on the same host, though the docblock does not mention this explicitly. ## Actual Behaviour The link was removed, along with its text. ## Steps to Reproduce 1. In an empty directory install the two packages: ``` npm install defuddle linkedom ``` 2. Save this as `example.mjs`: ```js import { parseHTML } from 'linkedom'; import { Defuddle } from 'defuddle/node'; const url = 'https://pages.example.com/acmelabs/posts/12345'; const filler = '

Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet consectetur adipiscing elit sed do eiusmod tempor incididunt ut labore et dolore magna aliqua ut enim ad minim veniam quis nostrud exercitation ullamco laboris.

'; const html = `Repro

Repro

${filler.repeat(3)}

A paragraph long enough to exceed the rule's ten-word limit, ending with links to our profile and our other posts.

${filler.repeat(3)}
`; const { document } = parseHTML(html); const result = await Defuddle(document, url, { separateMarkdown: true }); console.log('off-site link kept:', result.content.includes('social.example.net/acme')); console.log('same-site link kept:', result.content.includes('our other posts')); console.log(result.contentMarkdown.split('\n').find(line => line.includes('ten-word limit'))); ``` 3. Run it: ``` node example.mjs ``` Output: ``` off-site link kept: false same-site link kept: false A paragraph long enough to exceed the rule's ten-word limit, ending with links to and . ``` Both ``s, both links, and the words "our profile" and "our other posts" are all gone, leaving the sentence ending on a bare full stop. Two markup conditions are needed to reach the rule, which is why the issue doesn't always present: the link must sit inside a **wrapper element** (a bare `` in flowing prose is exempted by the rule's own `closest('p')` guard), and the paragraph must **exceed ten words** (a shorter one is itself matched and removed whole, so the symptom looks like a missing paragraph rather than a missing link). ## Root Cause In `src/removals/content-patterns.ts` ~L800: ```ts const linkPath = new URL(link.getAttribute('href') || '', url).pathname; // ... if (linkPath !== '/' && linkPath !== urlPath && (urlPath.startsWith(linkPath) || isParentIndex)) { el.remove(); } ``` Two guards are missing, and the example above hits both: **1. The host is never compared.** `linkPath` is only a pathname, so a link to any site is eligible. `pageHost` is already computed a few lines above and goes unused until the trailing external-link rule further down. **2. The prefix has no segment boundary.** `urlPath.startsWith(linkPath)` matches mid-segment, so `/blog/20` counts as a parent of `/blog/2024/post`. A prefix should count only when the next character is `/`, or when `linkPath` already ends in one. The other branch, `isParentIndex`, strips back to the last `/` to build a directory path, so it already ends at a separator and is unaffected. They are independent: fixing only the host still deletes a same-site link to `/acme` from a page at `/acmelabs/posts/12345` — the second link in the example above. ## Next Steps I have a fix for both guards — one commit each, so either can be dropped — and will open a PR against `main`. Searched open and closed issues and PRs for `breadcrumb`, `"section breadcrumb"`, `removeByContentPattern`, `startsWith` and `pathname prefix` before filing; the nearest matches (#107, #134, #228, #252) all seem to be different mechanisms.

## Context

Defuddle is bundled into a Firefox WebExtension (a web clipper) submitted to addons.mozilla.org. AMO's validator (addons-linter, the same engine `web-ext lint` runs) flags three `UNSAFE_VAR_ASSIGNMENT` warnings, all inside Defuddle — the only `innerHTML` assignments in the whole bundle:

- `src/utils/dom.ts:31` — `decodeHTMLEntities`: `textarea.innerHTML = text`
- `src/utils/dom.ts:105` — `parseHTML`: `template.innerHTML = html`
- `src/utils/dom.ts:111` — `parseHTML` fallback: `div.innerHTML = html`

They are warnings, not errors ("Add-on passed validation"), and the idioms are safe — a detached `<textarea>` never executes anything, and `<template>` content is inert. But every extension that bundles Defuddle will carry these three warnings into AMO review, and addons-linter offers no inline suppression, so the only place to explain them is the reviewer notes of each add-on.

## Ask

Would you take a PR that keeps the exact same parsing semantics but avoids the `innerHTML` setter the linter matches on? Two candidates, both relying on `DOMParser` (available wherever `document` is, and in the linkedom path too?):

1. `decodeHTMLEntities`:
   ```ts
   const doc2 = new DOMParser().parseFromString(`<textarea>${text}</textarea>`, 'text/html');
   return (doc2.querySelector('textarea') as HTMLTextAreaElement).value;
   ```
   `<textarea>` is RCDATA in a full parse exactly as it is for the fragment case, so entity decoding matches — the one divergence is a literal `</textarea>` in the input.

2. `parseHTML`:
   ```ts
   const doc2 = new DOMParser().parseFromString(`<template>${html}</template>`, 'text/html');
   return doc2.querySelector('template')!.content;  // already inert
   ```
   A `<template>` in a full parse enters the same "in template" insertion mode the fragment algorithm uses for a template context, so the resulting tree is the same; again the edge is a literal `</template>` inside `html`.

If the edge cases make that unattractive, an alternative is to leave the code as-is and add a short note in the README for extension authors ("these three warnings are expected; here is what they are"), which downstream projects could link from their AMO reviewer notes.

Happy to open the PR with tests for both functions (including the edge cases above) if either direction works for you. Thanks for Defuddle — it's doing the heavy lifting of an Evernote-grade clipper very well.

**Defuddle version:** 0.19.2 **Repository:** https://github.com/kepano/defuddle ## Summary Defuddle silently drops content inside HTML elements with `data-component-part` attributes (such as `data-component-part="step-content"` and `data-component-part="step-title"`) when those elements appear anywhere inside an ancestor with `role="list"`. This affects pages rendered by Mintlify's documentation framework, which uses custom React/MDX Step and Steps components that serialize to `role="list"` containers with `data-component-part` children. The content is simply absent from the Markdown output — there is no warning, placeholder, or any indication that content was skipped. Content with `data-component-part` but **without** a `role="list"` ancestor is handled correctly regardless of nesting depth. I encountered this problem when using obsidian clipper on https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices#explore-first-then-plan-then-code, noticing that some content was dropped. ## Example Input ```html

Before.

Title

Content

After.

``` ## Expected Output ```markdown Before. Title Content After. ``` (Or some other reasonable Markdown representation of the structured list content.) ## Actual Output Running `npx defuddle parse input.html --md` produces: ```markdown Before. After. ``` The heading and the three `

` elements inside `data-component-part="step-content"` are all **silently dropped** — no warning, no empty placeholder, nothing. ## Bug Notes Content extraction within `data-component-part` elements is **not universally dropped**. It depends on the nesting context. ### Concrete Output (verified with defuddle 0.19.2) **`output_source_excerpt.txt`** — Real-world Steps component HTML: Only the intro paragraph and ending paragraph survive in the output: ``` ## Test: Steps component content dropped The following content is wrapped in custom Step/Steps component markup... This paragraph is after the Steps component and should appear in the output. ``` All three Step items (Explore, Plan, Code) with their titles, paragraphs, and code blocks are **completely absent** — no trace in the output. **`output_test_comprehensive.txt`** — Nesting-depth tests: ``` Standard paragraph at the start. Test 1: Direct child of body Test 2: One wrapper div deep Test 3: Two wrapper divs deep Test 4: Inside role="listitem" Test 5: nested deeper in listitem Test 9: listitem only, no data-component-part Standard paragraph at the end. ``` Only T6, T7, and T8 are truly absent (their text does not appear in the output at all). All other tests produce output. ### Test Results A comprehensive nesting-depth test (`test_comprehensive.html`) was run against defuddle 0.19.2. Note: the `--md` flag is not recognized (output is plain text, not Markdown-formatted). #### Concrete nesting patterns table | Test | Structure | Visible? | |------|-----------|----------| | T1 | `body > div[data-component-part]` | Appears | | T2 | `body > div > div[data-component-part]` | Appears | | T3 | `body > div > div > div[data-component-part]` | Appears | | T4 | `body > div[role="listitem"] > div[data-component-part]` | Appears | | T5 | `body > div[role="listitem"] > div > div[data-component-part]` | Appears | | T6 | `body > div[role="list"] > div[role="listitem"] > div[data-component-part]` | **Dropped** | | T7 | `body > div[role="list"] > div[role="listitem"] > div > div[data-component-part]` | **Dropped** | | T8 | `body > div[role="list"] > div > div[data-component-part]` | **Dropped** | | T9 | `body > div[role="listitem"]` (no `data-component-part`) | Appears | | Steps | Real Steps component (`role="list"` > listitem > data-component-part) | **All step content dropped** | ### Corrected Pattern The bug is **specifically tied to `role="list"` ancestry**. Content is dropped only when a `data-component-part` element appears **anywhere inside an ancestor with `role="list"`** (T6, T7, T8). Without a `role="list"` ancestor, `data-component-part` elements are handled correctly regardless of depth: direct children of `` (T1), nested in wrapper divs (T2, T3), inside `role="listitem"` alone (T4, T5), or anywhere else — all produce output. The key trigger is that defuddle's tree traversal has a special handler for `role="list"` elements, and within that handler, `data-component-part` children are either: - Not recursed into at all - Or their content is collapsed/cleared during the list-processing logic A `role="listitem"` element without an enclosing `role="list"` does NOT trigger the bug. ## Possible Root Cause (Code Analysis) Looking at the `md.ts` source code in defuddle 0.19.2, the likely bug location is in the **`extractContent` function's handler for `role="list"` elements**. The function has a special code path that processes `role="list"` containers: it iterates over child elements (expected to be `role="listitem"`), but when those child elements contain `data-component-part` attributes, the content extraction enters a code path that drops them. The probable flow: 1. Function enters a `role="list"` element 2. It finds child elements and processes each one with list-item handling logic 3. Inside list-item handling, `data-component-part` children are either: - Skipped because the list handler assumes all content is in direct text children, not in attribute-tagged divs - Or collapsed/cleared by the `data-component-part` inline-child collapse logic being applied at the wrong scope The fact that all nesting contexts inside `role="list"` are affected (T6-T8) — regardless of depth — suggests the `role="list"` handler simply doesn't recurse into child elements that carry `data-component-part` attributes, rather than a depth-sensitive collapse bug. ## Reproduction ```bash # Save the example HTML above as test.html, then run: npx defuddle parse test.html --md ``` [minimal_example.html](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30366494/minimal_example.html) [output_minimal_example.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30366495/output_minimal_example.txt) [test_comprehensive.html](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30366497/test_comprehensive.html) [output_test_comprehensive.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30366496/output_test_comprehensive.txt)

### Summary

`defuddle parse --markdown <youtube-url>` reliably fails with `ERR_INVALID_URL` (`new URL("undefined")`) inside `MetadataExtractor.extract` when run in a Linux container (Railway/Nixpacks), while the exact same command, same pinned dependency versions, succeeds every time on macOS locally. Not fixed by changing the Node version (tried 20.18.0 and 22.x — same failure on both).

### Environment where it fails

- defuddle `0.19.1`
- Node `20.18.0`, also reproduced on `22.x` — Nixpacks-built container (Debian-based, `linux/amd64`), deployed on Railway
- Dependencies pinned via lockfile: `linkedom@0.18.12`, `mathml-to-latex@1.8.0`, `temml@0.13.3`, `turndown@7.2.0`, `commander@^12.1.0`

### Environment where it works

- Same defuddle version (`0.19.1`), same lockfile-pinned dependency versions
- macOS, Node `v24.13.0`
- 100% success rate across many repeated runs against the same video URL

### Steps to reproduce

```bash
defuddle parse --markdown "https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0YeeJHYy-Vc"
```

- On macOS/Node 24: succeeds, returns full transcript + 9 chapter headers.
- On the Linux container/Node 20 or 22: exits 0 (no crash), but the output has no `## Transcript` section at all — just the frontmatter. stderr contains:

```
Failed to parse URL: TypeError: Invalid URL
    at new URL (node:internal/url:806:29)
    at MetadataExtractor.extract (dist/metadata.js:24:30)
    at Defuddle.tryAsyncExtractor (dist/defuddle.js:662:63)
    at process.processTicksAndRejections (node:internal/process/task_queues:95:5)
    at async Defuddle.parseAsync (dist/defuddle.js:619:33)
    at async Defuddle (dist/node.js:71:20)
    at async parseSource (dist/cli.js:65:18)
    at async Command.<anonymous> (dist/cli.js:156:32) {
  code: 'ERR_INVALID_URL',
  input: 'undefined'
}
```

...and a second, near-identical occurrence from the bot-UA retry path:

```
Failed to parse URL: TypeError: Invalid URL
    at new URL (node:internal/url:806:29)
    at async parseSource (dist/cli.js:83:35)
    at async Command.<anonymous> (dist/cli.js:156:32) {
  code: 'ERR_INVALID_URL',
  input: 'undefined'
}
```

### What I think is happening

`input: 'undefined'` is the literal *string* `"undefined"`, not JS `undefined` — so something is stringifying an unset value before it reaches `new URL()`. In `metadata.js`:

```js
url = doc.location?.href || '';
```

My guess is `doc.location.href` (from `linkedom`'s parsed document, built without an explicit base URL in `parseLinkedomHTML`) is coming back as the string `"undefined"` rather than an empty string or real `undefined`, so the `|| ''` fallback never kicks in, and the later `new URL(url)` call throws.

This is caught internally (`console.warn`, not fatal) inside `MetadataExtractor.extract` — but the *second* occurrence, at `cli.js:83` (inside the bot-UA retry branch), does not appear to be inside a try/catch that recovers gracefully, and the net effect is that `result.wordCount === 0` on both the initial and bot-UA-retried parse, so the CLI silently returns content with no transcript section at all instead of erroring loudly.

### Not Node-version-specific, and confirmed content-dependent (not a guess)

I initially suspected a Node 20 vs Node 24 API difference (e.g. WHATWG URL parsing strictness), but bumping the container's pinned Node from 20.18.0 to 22.x produced the identical failure — same stack trace, same `input: 'undefined'`.

To actually confirm the content-difference theory rather than just guess at it, I fetched the exact same URL with the exact same User-Agent header defuddle uses, from both environments, and diffed the raw response:

| | From the working environment (macOS, residential IP) | From the failing environment (Railway, datacenter IP) |
|---|---|---|
| HTTP status | 200 | 200 |
| Response size | 1,327,935 bytes | 1,201,756 bytes (~10% smaller) |
| `<title>` tag | `The Correct Way to Build and Manage AI Agents in 47 Minutes \| Jared Zoneraich - YouTube` | `- YouTube` (**empty**) |
| `lang` attribute | `en-GB` | `en` |
| `ytInitialPlayerResponse` occurrences | 3 | 3 |

Both responses are 200 OK and both superficially look like a YouTube watch page (present `ytInitialPlayerResponse`), but the datacenter-IP response is missing the video title and is meaningfully smaller — i.e. YouTube is serving an incompletely-hydrated/degraded page render to that IP, not a hard block page, but not the real page either. That's almost certainly what's putting `linkedom`'s parsed `doc.location`/metadata into the broken state that trips `new URL("undefined")` downstream — the bug is in how defuddle/linkedom handle *this specific degraded HTML shape*, not a Node-version issue, and not something under my control to prevent YouTube from sending.

### Ask

Given this is IP-reputation-driven content degradation on YouTube's side (not something I can fix from my end), I'd still find it useful to know:
1. Whether `doc.location.href` returning the string `"undefined"` from `linkedom` under this kind of degraded/incomplete HTML is a known quirk, and whether it's worth guarding against (e.g. treating a missing/empty `<title>` as a signal to retry or fail loudly rather than silently return `wordCount === 0` content).
2. Whether defuddle's bot-UA retry path (`cli.js:83`) is expected to help in this situation, since in my case it didn't — same degraded response on retry.

Happy to provide the two full HTML responses (or more diagnostics) if that'd help track it down.

An normalen Tagen spielen Kinder auf dem Schulhof der Joan-Baptista-Serra-Grundschule in Alcanar. Heute fahren Blaulichtfahrzeuge mit Sirenen auf den Hof. Der Katastrophenschutz ist zu Besuch. Denn statt Mathe oder Englisch steht ein neues Fach auf dem Stundenplan: der Klimaunterricht. Er soll seit diesem Schuljahr an allen Schulen Spaniens verpflichtend Kinder und Jugendliche auf die Auswirkungen der Klimakrise vorbereiten, praktisch und lebensnah. In kaum einem anderen Land ist die Anpassung an die Erderwärmung so schnell im Lehrplan angekommen. Auslöser dafür war eine der größten Naturkatastrophen in Spaniens Geschichte, gerade mal rund 150 Kilometer südwestlich der Serra-Grundschule. Im Oktober 2024 starben in der Region Valencia mehr als 220 Menschen durch eine Flut. Das Unglück traf die Region völlig unvorbereitet, die Regierung sah sich heftiger Kritik ausgesetzt. Währenddessen schreitet die Erderhitzung kaum gebremst voran, mit jedem Zehntelgrad wird die Anzahl von Waldbränden, Überschwemmungen oder Dürren in den nächsten Jahren weltweit zunehmen. Die Katastrophe von Valencia hat Spanien zum Handeln gebracht. Einen Monat nach der Überflutung verabschiedete die Regierung ein Gesetz, das Klimabildung verpflichtend macht. Eine aufgeklärte Bevölkerung rettet im Ernstfall Leben Während in Deutschland bei der Katastrophenprävention meist über teure Infrastruktur, neue Deiche oder Sirenen diskutiert wird, zeigt der spanische Vorstoß eine andere Dimension: Eine aufgeklärte Bevölkerung kostet den Staat kaum Geld, rettet im Ernstfall aber Leben. Entwickelt Spanien damit ein Bildungsmodell für die Zukunft? In Alcanar üben die Grund­schü­le­r:in­nen als Erstes, wie sie sich im Falle eines Feuers zu verhalten hätten. Die Feuerwehr betritt das Gebäude, ausgestattet mit Schutzausrüstung, Schläuchen und Rauchmasken. Aus den oberen Klassenzimmern winken ihnen die Schü­le­r:in­nen zu – sie wissen, dass es sich nur um eine Simulation handelt. Vom Schulhof aus beobachtet Mario González Jorge, Direktor der regionalen Bildungsbehörde, das Geschehen. „Wir merken schon lange, dass der Klimawandel im vollen Gange ist und die Extremwetterereignisse zunehmen“, sagt er. Deswegen unterstützt er den neuen Lehrplan. Die Schulkinder sollen lernen, wie sie Gefahrensituationen erkennen und sich schützen können. „Und das nicht nur in der Schule, sondern auch außerhalb.“ Wann ist es sicherer, in einem Gebäude zu bleiben, wann besser, schnell zu evakuieren? Dafür sollen die Grundschulkinder ein Gefühl entwickeln. Schon ab dem Vorschulalter finden mindestens zwei Unterrichtsstunden im Jahr statt. Das schreibt der Ausbildungsplan vor, den das Bildungs- und das Innenministerium gemeinsam erarbeitet haben. „Es geht darum, den Schü­le­r:in­nen angemessene Kenntnisse und Werte zu vermitteln, um Notfallsituationen effektiv und sicher zu bewältigen“, heißt es im Papier der Regierung. Spielerisch sollen Kinder dabei lernen, wie sie einen Alarm und erste Gefahrenzeichen erkennen. In der dritten und vierten Klasse besteht der Klimaunterricht aus vier Stunden im Jahr: drei Theorieeinheiten und eine praktische Übung. Ab dem kommenden Schuljahr soll der Lehrplan auch in den weiterführenden Schulen umgesetzt und möglicherweise um mehr Stunden erweitert werden. Der genaue Inhalt des Unterrichts wird an die geografische Lage der Schulen angepasst. In einem Dorf am Waldrand sollen die Schulkinder andere Schutzmaßnahmen lernen, als in einer Stadt am Meer. Wie in Deutschland ist das Thema Bildung in Spanien hauptsächlich Ländersache, allerdings darf die Zentralregierung in Madrid verbindliche Basislehrpläne für das ganze Land vorgeben. Die autonomen Regionen sind dafür zuständig, den Klimaunterricht nun konkret in ihre Lehrpläne einzubauen und ihre Leh­re­r:in­nen fortzubilden. Dass der praktische Unterricht in Alcanar – einer Stadt nahe des Mittelmeers, die selbst schon Überflutungen erlebt hat – ausgerechnet mit einer Feuerschutzübung beginnt, wirkt etwas paradox. Die Gründe dafür sind dann auch eher pragmatischer Natur. Feuerschutzübungen fanden hier wie auch in anderen Schulen schon vor der Einführung des neuen Unterrichts statt. Daher war das Brandszenario am einfachsten umzusetzen, während aufwendigere Simulationen erst noch vorbereitet werden müssen. Die Kinder lernen mit psychischen Belastungen umzugehen Zugleich erreicht die Zahl der Waldbrände in Spanien jährlich neue Rekord, gerade in den trockenen Regionen des Landes und bedingt durch die Klimakrise. Deshalb gehört der Brandschutz nun ganz offiziell zum Lehrplan. Auch die Vorbereitung auf Erdbeben, Flutwellen, Überflutungen oder Chemie- und Nuklearunfälle steht auf dem Programm. Neben konkreten Verhaltensweisen sollen die Schü­le­r:in­nen in Alcanar auch lernen, in Notfallsituationen Desinformationen zu erkennen und Krisen emotional zu bewältigen. Als die Feuerwehrleute nach einiger Zeit den fiktiven Brand gelöscht haben, warten die Schü­le­r:in­nen weiterhin in den oberen Stockwerken des Gebäudes ab. Gleichzeitig verlassen zwei Lehrerinnen die Schule und spielen eine Panikattacke vor. Ein Rettungssanitäter sorgt für emotionale Unterstützung. In weiteren Einheiten sollen auch die Schulkinder selbst lernen, wie sie mit den psychischen Belastungen einer Krise umgehen können. Ziel des neuen Lehrplans ist es, „die Schü­le­r:in­nen für die Bedeutung des emotionalen Wohlbefindens zu sensibilisieren“. Auch in Deutschland wurde längst beschlossen, dass Schulkinder mehr über die Klimakrise lernen sollen. Die Schul­mi­nis­te­r:in­nen aller Bundesländer haben 2017 dem Nationalen Aktionsplan Bildung für nachhaltige Entwicklung zugestimmt, wonach Nachhaltigkeit in „allen Bildungsbereichen strukturell verankert werden“ soll. Der Klimawandel wird in verschiedenen Fächern thematisiert, ein praktischer Unterricht wie in Spanien ist aber nicht offiziell vorgesehen. Politische Klimabildung kommt oft zu kurz Das liege auch daran, dass die Folgen der Klimakrise in Deutschland oft noch verdrängt werden, sagt Inga Feuser, zweite Bundesvorsitzende der Teachers for Future. Zwar häufen sich auch hierzulande die Extremwetterereignisse, aber so direkt wie südlichere Länder ist Deutschland noch nicht von extremen Dürren, Waldbränden und Hitzesommern betroffen. „Natürlich wird die Erderwärmung in den Schulen besprochen“, sagt Feuser, die selbst Deutsch, Geschichte und Religion an einem Gymnasium in Nordrhein-Westfalen unterrichtet, „aber wir wünschen uns einen größeren themenorientierten Fokus.“ Es sei für sie richtig, dass die Klimakrise aus unterschiedlichen Perspektiven statt in einem einzigen Fach beleuchtet werde. „Aber wenn wir in der siebten Klasse in Erdkunde darüber sprechen und in der achten in Physik, fehlen oft die Zusammenhänge.“ Der Hamburger Schülerin Nuria Neubauer ist das nicht genug. In einem Gastbeitrag in der Zeit stellt das Fridays-for-Future-Mitglied fest, dass Schulbehörden zwar langsam endlich Bildung für nachhaltige Entwicklung in die Lehrpläne inkludieren – aber vor allem mit dem Fokus, wie das eigene Handeln andere Menschen und Generationen beeinflusst und welche globalen Mechanismen zu Krieg führen können. „Ein Fach zur Vorbereitung auf Krisenmanagement und extreme Dürre, Hitze, Wasserknappheit, Starkregenfälle, Fluten und Waldbrände ist das also nicht.“ Laut einer Auswertung der Unesco haben etwa 70 Prozent aller jungen Menschen das Gefühl, nicht über genügend Wissen zu verfügen, um den Klimawandel zu verstehen. Umgekehrt fühlt sich auch nur ein Drittel aller Lehrkräfte weltweit überhaupt in der Lage, die lokalen Auswirkungen des Klimawandels im Unterricht angemessen zu erklären. Das soll sich in Deutschland ändern, indem „die Bedeutung von Bildung für nachhaltige Entwicklung verstärkt wird“. Das Bundeskabinett hat einen Indikator beschlossen, der Schulen nach ihrem Engagement misst. Im Schuljahr 2023/2024 hatte bundesweit etwa jede zehnte Schule das Thema Bildung für nachhaltige Entwicklung ausreichend im Unterricht und der Schule selbst etabliert. Udo Michallik, Generalsekretär der Kultusministerkonferenz, blickt optimistisch in die Zukunft: „Ich bin zuversichtlich, dass der Indikator noch weitere Schulen motiviert, Bildung für nachhaltige Entwicklung als orientierendes Konzept für Schulentwicklung zu verankern.“ Für Lehrerin Feuser reicht das noch nicht aus. Es sei zentral, die politische Bildung in Schulen zu verstärken. „Wir müssen Schü­le­r:in­nen bewusst machen, dass sie das Menschenrecht auf einen intakten Planeten haben und sie ermächtigen, dieses Recht einzufordern. Wie zynisch ist es, nur zu lehren: Wir verbrennen eure Welt, aber so könnt ihr damit umgehen.“ Unterricht zur emotionalen Bewältigung der Krise fehle in Deutschland ebenso wie zum sozialen Umgang miteinander in den kommenden Katastrophen. Damals wusste niemand, was zu tun war Auch beim Lehrpersonal in Alcanar herrscht Gewissheit, dass sich Extremwetterereignisse häufen werden. Die Schule liegt nicht weit vom Meer, sodass der steigende Wasserspiegel schon jetzt Sorgen bereitet. Nachdem Feuerwehr und Rettungswagen abgezogen sind und der gewohnte Unterricht weitergeht, fasst Mario González Jorge zusammen: „Wir wollen in der Schule für das Leben lernen. Und dazu gehört auch die Vorbereitung auf den Klimawandel.“ Vor fünf Jahren stand die Joan-Baptista-Serra-Schule nach Starkregenfällen bereits einmal unter Wasser. Die Flut war so heftig, dass Tische und Stühle aus der Stadt bis zum Meer gerissen wurden. Personen waren nicht direkt betroffen, aber die Leh­re­r:in­nen in Alcanar erinnern sich noch gut an das Chaos und den Schock in der Schule. „Damals wusste niemand, was zu tun war“, sagt die Lehrerin, die zuvor den Panikanfall simuliert hatte. Die Brandschutzübung sei für sie erst der Anfang. Für den Ernstfall will sie, dass alle wissen, wie sich die Schule schnell evakuieren ließe. Jetzt zumindest ein wenig besser vorbereitet zu sein, fühle sich beruhigend an.

**Symptom:** In Obsidian Web Clipper on iOS Safari, `{{transcript}}` is always empty for YouTube videos, while the same template works on macOS (www.youtube.com). Previously reported as symptoms in obsidianmd/obsidian-clipper#728 and obsidianmd/obsidian-clipper#758, but the underlying fetch bug was never identified. Verified against current `main` (9db7260).

## Root cause

On iPhone, Safari is redirected to `m.youtube.com`, so the caption XML fetch to `https://www.youtube.com/api/timedtext?...` is cross-origin. `fetchCaptionXml` attaches a custom header:

https://github.com/kepano/defuddle/blob/9db72600/src/extractors/youtube.ts#L585

```ts
const captionHeaders: Record<string, string> = { 'User-Agent': 'Mozilla/5.0' };
```

`User-Agent` is no longer a forbidden header in WebKit, so the browser does not strip it. On a cross-origin request it is a non-safelisted header, which forces a CORS preflight. The timedtext endpoint's preflight response contains no `Access-Control-Allow-Headers`, so the request is blocked and the fetch rejects with `TypeError: Load failed`. The transcript then falls through to the mobile DOM-clicking fallback, which frequently fails (see "Secondary issues" below), so the user gets an empty transcript.

On desktop (www.youtube.com) the same fetch is same-origin, CORS never applies, and everything works. That is the entire macOS/iOS asymmetry.

## Reproduction (Playwright WebKit 26.4, which is the iOS Safari engine)

On a loaded `https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=dQw4w9WgXcQ` page, in page context:

| Step (mirrors youtube.ts logic) | Result |
| --- | --- |
| InnerTube `IOS` client POST to `/youtubei/v1/player` | PASS, status 200, 6 captionTracks |
| `fetch(track.baseUrl, { headers: { 'User-Agent': 'Mozilla/5.0' } })` | **FAIL, `TypeError: Load failed`** |
| Identical `fetch(track.baseUrl)` with no headers | PASS, status 200, 4555 bytes of transcript XML |

Preflight evidence via curl (note: no `Access-Control-Allow-Headers` in the response, so the requested `user-agent` header is not approved):

```
$ curl -X OPTIONS "https://www.youtube.com/api/timedtext?..." \
    -H "Origin: https://m.youtube.com" \
    -H "Access-Control-Request-Method: GET" \
    -H "Access-Control-Request-Headers: user-agent" -D -
HTTP/2 200
access-control-allow-origin: https://m.youtube.com
access-control-allow-credentials: true
```

## Suggested fix

Only set the `User-Agent` header outside browser contexts (it exists for the server-side CLI; in a browser the real UA is sent anyway and the custom value is at best ignored):

```ts
const captionHeaders: Record<string, string> = {};
if (typeof window === 'undefined') {
    captionHeaders['User-Agent'] = 'Mozilla/5.0';
}
```

The same consideration applies to the Android InnerTube client path in `fetchPlayerData`, which also sends a custom `User-Agent` and cannot pass preflight from `m.youtube.com` (the player endpoint's preflight only allows `content-type`). The IOS client path is unaffected since `Content-Type: application/json` is approved.

## Secondary issues found while diagnosing (can split into separate issues if preferred)

1. **Relative inline `baseUrl` on m.youtube.com.** The mobile page's `ytInitialPlayerResponse` caption `baseUrl` is relative (`/api/timedtext?...`), so the SSRF guard `new URL(track.baseUrl)` throws and kills the inline path even though that fetch would be same-origin on mobile. Fix: `new URL(track.baseUrl, 'https://www.youtube.com')` (https://github.com/kepano/defuddle/blob/9db72600/src/extractors/youtube.ts#L582).
2. **Mobile DOM fallback rarely fires.** `openMobileTranscriptPanel` requires `button[aria-label="View all"]`, which only exists when the video has chapters, and the full chain (3 sequential 4s API attempts plus up to 5s polling per step) can exceed Obsidian Web Clipper's 8s `parseAsync` race, after which the sync fallback drops async variables like `{{transcript}}` while all sync variables fill in normally. That matches the "everything but the transcript" reports exactly.

Happy to submit a PR for the User-Agent and relative-URL fixes if useful.
title: YouTube transcript fails on iOS Safari (m.youtube.com): User-Agent header on caption fetch breaks CORS preflight

body: **Describe the bug** When clipping articles from ScienceDirect (https://www.sciencedirect.com/), all inline citation references in the article body are rendered as empty brackets or empty parentheses in the output Markdown. The citation text (e.g. Abascal et al., 2022) is completely lost. **Root cause** ScienceDirect wraps all anchor link text in a two-level nested span structure: ``` Abascal et al., 2022 ``` The Web Clipper's HTML→Markdown converter appears to read only the direct child text nodes of `` elements, and does not recursively extract text from nested` `children. As a result, the link text is empty and the citation collapses to` () `or` [] `in the output. This pattern is used consistently and site-wide on ScienceDirect — not just for citations, but for all interactive anchor elements. Running the following in DevTools confirms 440 instances on a single article page: ``` document.querySelectorAll('.anchor.anchor-primary .anchor-text') // NodeList(440) [span.anchor-text, span.anchor-text, ...] ```
title: Inline citation link text lost when converting ScienceDirect articles (nested .anchor-text-container > .anchor-text pattern)

## Summary

`fetchPage` currently sends the following `Accept` header:

```
Accept: text/html,application/xhtml+xml
```

This means servers that support content negotiation — such as GitHub raw URLs, many documentation sites, and any server implementing the [`text/markdown` media type (RFC 7763)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7763) — will always respond with HTML, even when they could serve markdown directly.

## Suggestion

Expand the `Accept` header to include `text/markdown` with a higher or equal priority:

```
Accept: text/markdown,text/html,application/xhtml+xml
```

If the server responds with `Content-Type: text/markdown`, defuddle could skip the HTML parsing and extraction pipeline entirely and pass the body straight through — potentially producing cleaner output with less processing overhead.

## Current behavior

Even when `--md` is passed, defuddle always fetches HTML and converts it locally via `extractRawMarkdown` / the markdown pipeline. There is no path for receiving native markdown from the server.

## Notes

- `extractRawMarkdown` already exists in `fetch.js` and uses heuristics (`isMarkdownContent`) to detect markdown embedded in HTML — native content negotiation would be a more reliable signal.
- This would be a no-op for the vast majority of servers that don't support `text/markdown`; they would simply ignore the additional `Accept` value.
- Care may be needed around how a raw markdown response is passed through vs. processed, since the current pipeline assumes HTML input.
title: Feature request: include text/markdown in Accept header to enable content negotiation

body:
## The problem

`defuddle parse <url>` fails on a significant number of sites because the [default User-Agent string](https://github.com/kepano/defuddle/blob/main/src/fetch.ts#L7) is recognized as a bot by CDN and WAF providers (Akamai, Cloudflare, etc.). These providers either tarpit the connection (never respond, triggering the 10s timeout) or reject it outright with a 403.

The CLI currently has no way to override the User-Agent, so there's no workaround short of patching `node_modules`.

### Example sites

I tested ~50 sites across news, tech, entertainment, and gaming. Most work fine. But a handful of major properties (presumably behind CDN-level bot detection) fail consistently with defuddle's UA and succeed immediately with a browser UA:

| Site | defuddle UA | Browser UA |
|---|---|---|
| `minecraft.net` | `Timed out fetching page after 10s` | 200 OK |
| `cbc.ca` | `Timed out fetching page after 10s` | 200 OK |
| `washingtonpost.com` | `Timed out fetching page after 10s` | 200 OK |
| `npr.org` | `Timed out fetching page after 10s` | 200 OK |

The pattern is consistent: the CDN receives the request and silently tarpits the connection rather than responding. Node's native `fetch()` with no custom headers returns 200 immediately for all of these. The same request with defuddle's UA hangs until the 10s timeout fires. Swap in a Chrome- or Firefox-like UA string and it works again. The sites aren't down: they're just refusing to talk to a declared bot.

It is worth noting that `bloomberg.com` returns 403 regardless of UA (I suspect that it makes use of deeper JS/cookie-based protection), so this isn't a universal fix. But the tarpit pattern above is clearly UA-driven and affects enough mainstream sites to be worth addressing.

### Reproduction

Any of the sites above will reproduce, but here's a quick isolated test:

```bash
# defuddle's UA — times out
node -e "
fetch('https://www.cbc.ca/radio/costofliving/booze-free-costly-9.6969478', {
  headers: {
    'User-Agent': 'Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; Defuddle/1.0; +https://defuddle.md)',
    'Accept': 'text/html,application/xhtml+xml'
  },
  signal: AbortSignal.timeout(15000)
}).then(r => console.log(r.status, r.statusText))
  .catch(e => console.error(e.message));
"
# → "The operation was aborted due to timeout"

# browser UA — immediate 200
node -e "
fetch('https://www.cbc.ca/radio/costofliving/booze-free-costly-9.6969478', {
  headers: {
    'User-Agent': 'Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/125.0.0.0 Safari/537.36',
    'Accept': 'text/html,application/xhtml+xml'
  },
  signal: AbortSignal.timeout(15000)
}).then(r => console.log(r.status, r.statusText))
  .catch(e => console.error(e.message));
"
# → "200 OK"
```

**Version:** 0.16.0, Node 20+, Windows 11

## Context: existing UA and retry logic

The current UA string and retry logic were introduced in [33738d6](https://github.com/kepano/defuddle/commit/33738d6) (fixing #178). That commit consolidated fetch logic into `src/fetch.ts` and added a smart retry: if the initial fetch returns zero words, the CLI retries with a bot UA (`Defuddle/1.0 ... bot`). This handles sites like Obsidian Publish that serve pre-rendered content to bots.

That's the right call for cooperative sites that *want* to serve good content to bots. The problem I'm running into is the inverse - sites that treat any non-browser UA as hostile and either tarpit or reject the request. The current retry logic never gets a chance to fire because the initial fetch itself fails.

## Proposal

I see two possible approaches. They aren't mutually exclusive.

### Option A: `--user-agent` flag

Add a CLI option to override the default UA:

```bash
defuddle parse <url> --md --user-agent "Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) ..."
```

This is the minimal change - it gives callers control without changing defuddle's default behavior. The existing `getInitialUA()` / bot-retry logic stays exactly as-is; the flag just overrides the starting UA when provided.

### Option B: internal retry with browser UA on timeout/403

The CLI already has retry logic for the "empty content" case ([lines 78-104](https://github.com/kepano/defuddle/blob/main/src/cli.ts#L78-L104) of `cli.ts`). A symmetric retry could handle the "blocked UA" case:

1. First attempt uses the current default UA (honest identification)
2. If the response is a timeout or 403, retry with a hardcoded browser-like UA
3. All other errors (DNS failure, 404, content-type mismatch, etc.) fail immediately - no retry

This would be the inverse of the existing bot-UA retry: that one escalates *toward* a bot identity for cooperative sites, this one escalates *toward* a browser identity for hostile ones.

I suspect this option might not sit well with everyone - it's a bit duplicitous, and there's a reasonable argument that defuddle should identify itself honestly and let the site decide. I get that. But it's worth considering because of how it interacts with programmatic callers (see below).

### Why this matters for programmatic callers

I stumbled into this while evaluating a [Claude Code skill](https://github.com/kepano/obsidian-skills/blob/main/skills/defuddle/SKILL.md) that uses defuddle as its web fetching layer. The skill teaches an AI coding assistant to run `defuddle parse <url> --md` instead of fetching raw HTML, which seems ideal for my Obsidian+Claude workflow, but the skill has no good way to handle UA-based failures. With a `--user-agent` flag (Option A), a skill could implement retry logic like:

```
1. Run: defuddle parse <url> --md
2. If stderr contains "Timed out" or "403": Retry: defuddle parse <url> --md --user-agent "<browser UA>"
3. All other errors: report failure, don't retry
```

This works, but it means every caller that wraps defuddle needs to independently implement the same timeout-detection-and-retry pattern. If defuddle handled the retry internally (Option B), the skill would just be `defuddle parse <url> --md` and it would work. 

## Offering to contribute

I'm happy to put together a PR for either or both options if the maintainers are open to this direction. I wanted to open the discussion first because I can see an argument that the default UA is a deliberate choice about how defuddle identifies itself, and I don't want to propose a change that cuts against the project's values. Curious to hear what others think.
title: Default User-Agent silently blocked by CDN/WAF bot detection on many sites

I’d like to propose a feature that would make it even more useful for archiving and offline usage.

### Feature request

Add support for:

1. **Downloading images referenced in Markdown**
	- Detect all image links in the Markdown (e.g. `![alt](https://example.com/image.png)`)
		- Download those images locally
2. **Rewriting image paths**
	- Replace remote URLs with local relative paths (e.g. `./images/image.png`)
3. **Configurable output location**
	- Allow specifying where downloaded assets are stored
		- For example, store them in a subfolder relative to the Markdown file, such as:
		- `./attachments/`
				- `./assets/images/`
4. **Configurable filename format (optional)**
	- Allow customizing how downloaded files are named
		- For example: `{page-name}-1.png`
		- This helps keep filenames meaningful and avoids collisions

### Example

**Input Markdown:**

```markdown
![Example](https://example.com/image.png)
```

**Output Markdown (custom folder + naming):**

```markdown
![Example](./attachments/example-page-1.png)
```

With the image saved locally:

```markdown
attachments/example-page-1.png
```

这不 DeepSeek 前脚刚刚上新了一篇关于推理时Scaling Law的论文嘛，引得大家纷纷联想是不是R2马上要来了。

然鹅……奥特曼这边却发了一条“变卦”的消息：

至于大家翘首以盼的 GPT-5 ，奥特曼表示：

将在几个月之后，而且效果会比我们最初设想的还要好。

至于原因，奥特曼也做出了解释。

大概意思就是，顺利整合所有内容比他们想象的要困难得多，希望确保有足够的能力来支持预期的需求。



咱就是说啊，现在真的是DeepSeek这边一有点声响，OpenAI那边就得有点动作来紧跟一下了。

DeepSeek新论文

在这个小插曲之后呢，我们还是把目光聚焦在DeepSeek这篇新论文身上。

这篇论文的名字叫做Inference-Time Scaling for Generalist Reward Modeling，由DeepSeek和清华大学共同提出。



这篇研究核心的亮点，就是提出了一个叫做 SPCT 方法 （Self-Principled Critique Tuning）的方法——

首次提出通过在线强化学习（RL）优化原则和批判生成，实现推理时扩展。

之所以要做这么一项研究，是因为之前大家用奖励模型（Reward Model, RM）在RL中为大语言模型生成奖励信号。

但现有的RM在通用领域却表现出受限的情况，尤其是在面对复杂、多样化任务的时候。

因此，就出现了两个关键挑战点。

一个是通用RM需要灵活性（支持单响应、多响应评分）和准确性（跨领域高质量奖励）。

另一个则是现有RM（如标量RM、半标量RM）在推理时扩展性差，无法通过增加计算资源显著提升性能。



为了解决这个问题，DeepSeek和清华大学团队便提出了SPCT。



整体来看，这项研究主要包含三大核心技术点。

首先就是 生成式奖励模型 （GRM）。

它采用点式生成奖励模型（Pointwise GRM），通过生成文本形式的奖励（如critiques）而非单一标量值，支持灵活输入（单响应、多响应）和推理时扩展。



其中，C是生成的critique，fextract从中提取分数。

接下来，是关键的SPCT了。

主要是通过在线强化学习（RL）训练GRM，使其能动态生成高质量的原则（principles）和批判（critiques），从而提升奖励质量。

整体来看，SPCT是一个两阶段的过程，它们分别是：

  • 拒绝式微调（Rejective Fine-Tuning）
  • ：冷启动阶段，通过采样和拒绝策略生成初始数据。
  • 基于规则的在线RL
  • ：使用规则化奖励函数优化原则和批判的生成，鼓励模型区分最佳响应。

在此基础上，便是第三个技术点，即推理时扩展技术。

先是通过多次采样生成多样化的原则和批判，投票聚合最终奖励，扩展奖励空间。

再训练一个辅助模型过滤低质量采样，进一步提升扩展效果。

基于上述的方法，团队也对结果做了一波测试。

在Reward Bench、PPE、RMB等基准上，DeepSeek-GRM-27B显著优于基线方法（如LLM-as-a-Judge、标量RM），且通过推理时扩展（32次采样）性能进一步提升（如Reward Bench准确率从86.0%提升至90.4%）。



总而言之，这篇研究证明了推理时扩展在通用RM中的有效性，性能超越训练时扩展。
